strengths: Interesting and creative core idea: procedurally generating simple 'Cézanne toy' primitives (spheres, cuboids, cylinders, rings) as a scalable, cheap training distribution for grasping, motivated by developmental psychology.

Extensive empirical validation across simulation and two distinct real robot embodiments (Franka arm with parallel gripper, Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands), with consistent gains over strong VLA baselines (OpenVLA-OFT, π0-FAST) despite orders of magnitude less data and a much smaller model (86M vs 3B/7B parameters).

Thorough ablation studies: pooling mechanism (DetPool vs attention/CLS/mean pooling), model size, number/diversity of toys vs number of demonstrations, importance of individual primitives, toy complexity, and color diversity — these provide good insight into what drives generalization.

Reasonably clear architecture description and detailed appendices (toy manufacturing process, hardware configurations, training hyperparameters, baseline implementation details, evaluation protocols) that aid reproducibility.

Results engage directly with a real and practically important problem (zero-shot generalization in manipulation) and offer a scalable, low-cost data-generation recipe that could be useful to the community.
weaknesses: LEGO's DetPool mechanism relies on test-time object segmentation masks (via SAM2 or a trained detector), essentially providing privileged object-localization information that the baseline VLA models do not receive; this makes the comparison to π0-FAST/OpenVLA-OFT somewhat unequal and complicates the 'zero-shot generalization' narrative, since success partly hinges on a separate, non-trivial perception module rather than the policy itself.

Evaluation is restricted to a single skill (pick-and-lift grasping) with a coarse success criterion (lifting above a height threshold); it remains unclear whether the object-centric representation and toy-based training generalize to more dexterous, contact-rich, or multi-step manipulation tasks.

Some baseline results appear weak relative to expectations (e.g., OpenVLA-OFT degrading with more data, π0-FAST needing large in-domain finetuning to be competitive), raising questions about whether baselines were optimally tuned; the paper's own explanation (overfitting, domain gap) is plausible but not deeply diagnosed.

The scaling and ablation studies, while useful, are conducted only in simulation, leaving open whether the same trends (e.g., diminishing returns from more demos vs. toy diversity) hold in the real-world settings where the headline results are reported.

Limited discussion of failure modes and error analysis (e.g., what kinds of real objects the model fails on, or how sensitive results are to segmentation mask quality/errors), which would strengthen understanding of the method's robustness limits.

The main contribution (a compositional-primitive dataset generation strategy plus attention-masked pooling) is somewhat incremental relative to existing object-centric representation literature (e.g., OTTER), and the paper's positioning against that closest related work is fairly brief.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated research question inspired by developmental cognitive science: can a robot policy generalize to novel real-world objects after training only on simple, randomly composed 'toy' primitives (spheres, cuboids, cylinders, rings)? The framing and the constructed 'Cezanne toys' dataset is a creative and potentially useful contribution to the community.

The proposed DetPool mechanism (masking ViT attention to object patches, then mean-pooling object tokens) is simple, lightweight, and clearly explained, and is shown via ablation to be substantially better than attention/CLS/mean pooling baselines across a wide range of demo counts (Table 1).

Extensive empirical evaluation across three platforms (ManiSkill simulation, Franka+Robotiq gripper on YCB, Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands), with comparisons to strong, much larger pretrained baselines (pi0-FAST 3B, OpenVLA-OFT 7B) and additional object-centric baselines (ShapeGrasp, GROOT, DexGraspVLA).

Numerous informative ablation/scaling studies: number and diversity of training toys, model size, primitive-type importance, toy complexity, geometric similarity (Chamfer distance) between train/test objects, condition/prediction horizon, delta vs absolute control, and color diversity.
A dedicated robustness study (lighting, clutter, distractors, mask noise) strengthens the claim that the object-centric representation is not brittle.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed appendices on toy manufacturing (printer settings), hardware configurations, teleoperation protocols, and baseline implementation/hyperparameters.

The core claim of data efficiency (86M-parameter model trained from scratch on 1.5K real demos matching or beating multi-billion-parameter VLAs in zero-shot settings) is a meaningful and practically relevant finding for the field.
weaknesses: The abstract's claim of 'outperforming state-of-the-art approaches' is partially overstated: on the real Franka benchmark (Table 2), the finetuned pi0-FAST actually beats LEGO (76.56% vs 66.67%), a fact only clarified in the body text, not reflected in the abstract framing.

The method's practical 'zero-shot' generalization depends on an external object segmentation/detection pipeline (SAM2 in the real world, or a separately trained Faster R-CNN detector for bounding boxes) to identify the target object at inference time. This adds a non-trivial dependency that is not deeply analyzed (e.g., failure cases when detection is wrong on truly novel objects) and somewhat complicates the 'grasp anything zero-shot' narrative.

Core technical novelty is incremental: DetPool is a masked-attention + mean-pooling variant conceptually similar to prior object-centric approaches (e.g., OTTER, cited as most similar); the main novelty is largely empirical/dataset-driven rather than algorithmic.

Most quantitative results (simulation and real-robot tables) are reported as single numbers without variance/confidence intervals or multiple seeds, except for Table 6; given real-robot trials are limited (16 or fewer per object), this limits statistical confidence in reported success-rate differences, especially the narrow margins in some baseline comparisons.

Baseline comparisons are not fully matched in training/pretraining budget (e.g., pi0-FAST pretrained on large-scale pi/DROID data vs LEGO trained from scratch), which is acknowledged but still makes some 'outperforming SOTA' claims less like-for-like, since the comparison conflates architecture, pretraining scale, and fine-tuning data simultaneously.

Task diversity is narrow: nearly all experiments are single-object pick/lift grasping (plus one push-to-target task in the appendix); the generalization claims are therefore scoped to grasping and not validated on more complex or long-horizon manipulation.
The H1-2 dexterous-hand evaluation was limited in scope due to hardware issues (unresponsive thumb joints), reducing confidence in the humanoid generalization claims relative to the Franka results.

The paper does not discuss failure modes or qualitative analysis of when/why the object-centric representation fails to generalize (e.g., which YCB objects failed and why), which would strengthen understanding of the method's limits beyond the 'easy/medium/hard' Chamfer-distance bucketing.
